title_r: Evaluations of Foreign-Made Products in a Limited Choice Environment: A Replication and Extension of the Direct Mediation Model
abstract_r: Situations where a market offers only foreign-produced products are becoming more and more common. Nonetheless, little research has focused on this interesting development. This study validates and extends a dual mediation hypothesis for foreign-made product evaluations. It offers insights into how ethnocentric tendencies influence attitudes and purchase intentions of a foreign brand where the available products in the consumer’s choice-set are all foreign made. The results show that country of origin-related cognitive responses influence attitude toward the ad and attitude toward the brand with differing intensity under conditions of high or low ethnocentrism and country of origin. The study provides some insights into the process of structural configurations of the relationships among cognitive response dimensions and purchase intentions and into the processes underlying how consumers evaluate foreign-made products.

title_r: Linking Personality Traits to Mediterranean Diet Adherence and Exploring Gene–Diet Interactions in Neuroticism
abstract_r: Background and Objectives: There is adherence to a healthy Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), but adherence varies widely. Precision nutrition is increasingly interested in individual characteristics influencing diet adherence, but few studies have examined personality traits. Our main aim was to investigate the association between personality traits and MedDiet adherence. Our secondary aims were to explore genome-wide genetic variants associated with neuroticism, including replication of previous findings, as well as to explore gene–MedDiet interactions. Methods: We analyzed participants (aged 55–75) in the PREDIMED-Plus-Valencia study and measured clinical, lifestyle, and genetic factors. The Eysenck Personality Questionnaire-Revised (EPQ-R) was used to measure neuroticism, psychoticism, and extraversion. Genotyping was undertaken, and associations with candidate SNPs, genome-wide association studies (GWAS), genetic risk scores (GRS), and gene–MedDiet interactions were explored. Results: Neuroticism was inversely (beta = −0.09; p = 0.001) associated with adherence to the Mediterranean diet (MEDAS-17). Likewise, the probability of low MedDiet adherence increased neuroticism (OR: 1.27; 95% CI: 1.02–1.60; p = 0.031 per SD). In the GWAS for this trait, several SNPs surpassed the suggestive level of statistical significance. The most strongly associated was rs10181407-NDUFA10 (NADH dehydrogenase 1 alpha subcomplex subunit 10) (beta = −2.39; p = 2.70 × 10−6). The GRS for neuroticism was significantly associated with MedDiet adherence (beta = −0.18; p = 0.020), increasing the causality level. We replicated some candidate SNPs, and among them, the rs2243873-EHMT2 (euchromatic histone lysine methyltransferase 2) gene. The analysis of gene–MedDiet interactions revealed the role of these dietary modulations. Conclusions: Neuroticism was the personality trait most inversely associated with MedDiet adherence, suggesting its integration in precision nutrition analysis. Moreover, neuroticism-related genetics and MedDiet modulations will also be important.

title_r: Failure to Replicate Previous Reports of Associations Between Fluid Intelligence and EEG Signal Complexity and Microstates: A Preregistered Study in a Large Sample
abstract_r: Resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) dynamics have been proposed as neural markers of individual cognitive abilities. Previous reports linked fluid intelligence with signal complexity derived from multivariate multiscale sample entropy and with microstate dynamics. In light of current concerns about low replicability rates in neuroscience, the present study aimed to replicate these previous results in a large data set (N = 582), while considering the short-term stability of resting-state spatiotemporal EEG features. Partial least squares regression was used to estimate the association between fluid intelligence and both signal complexity and microstate features. Whereas signal complexity was unrelated to fluid intelligence, certain features of microstates A and D were associated, although only in the female subsample. These results are partly consistent with those previously reported. However, retest correlations of both spatiotemporal features only displayed poor to acceptable stability across different resting-state measurements and conditions. Taken together, the current observations emphasize the need for more rigorous research practice and replication efforts in this research area.

title_r: Charting 15 years of progress in deep learning for speech emotion recognition: A replication study
abstract_r: Speech emotion recognition (SER) has long benefited from the adoption of deep learning methodologies. Deeper models -- with more layers and more trainable parameters -- are generally perceived as being `better' by the SER community. This raises the question -- \emph{how much better} are modern-era deep neural networks compared to their earlier iterations? Beyond that, the more important question of how to move forward remains as poignant as ever. SER is far from a solved problem; therefore, identifying the most prominent avenues of future research is of paramount importance. In the present contribution, we attempt a quantification of progress in the 15 years of research beginning with the introduction of the landmark 2009 INTERSPEECH Emotion Challenge. We conduct a large scale investigation of model architectures, spanning both audio-based models that rely on speech inputs and text-baed models that rely solely on transcriptions. Our results point towards diminishing returns and a plateau after the recent introduction of transformer architectures. Moreover, we demonstrate how perceptions of progress are conditioned on the particular selection of models that are compared. Our findings have important repercussions about the state-of-the-art in SER research and the paths forward

title_r: Global–local processing and the Ebbinghaus illusion: Group and individual differences in young and older adults
abstract_r: The Ebbinghaus illusion is a size illusion, in which a central circle appears larger or smaller depending on the size of surrounding circles. This illusion is widely used to study group-level differences in attentional processing, with the proposal that a local-processing bias reduces susceptibility to the Ebbinghaus illusion. One hundred and forty-five participants (87 young; 58 older) were included in the analyses. Participants completed the Navon hierarchical-figures task, to measure the global-local processing bias, and the Ebbinghaus illusion task, to measure susceptibility to the illusion. First, we investigated whether a strong local-processing bias reduced susceptibility to the Ebbinghaus illusion. Our findings did not support this proposal. At the group level, older participants demonstrated worse performance for global processing compared to young participants, but there were no age-group differences in susceptibility to the illusion. At the individual level, the young and older participants with the stronger local-processing bias were the participants with greater susceptibility to the illusion. Second, we investigated whether longer inspection times during the Ebbinghaus illusion task reduced susceptibility to the illusion. Our findings did support this proposal. At the group level, there were no age-group differences in either inspection time or susceptibility to the Ebbinghaus illusion. At the individual level, we replicated previous findings-the participants with the longer inspection times were the participants with the least susceptibility to the illusion. We discuss alternative cognitive mechanisms that may account for the Ebbinghaus illusion and their relevance to age-related changes and individual differences in visual attention.

title_r: A replication of an experiment "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning"
abstract_r: This project aims to replicate the seminal experiment from Murphy and Allopenna's (1994) study "On the Interaction of Theory and Data in Concept Learning," which investigates how theoretical knowledge influences the learning and categorization of concepts. The original study demonstrated that people do not merely rely on observable data to form categories but also use prior theoretical knowledge to guide their learning, interpretation, and generalization of concepts. In this replication, the objective is to validate the original findings by examining the interplay between theory-driven expectations and data-driven evidence during the process of concept acquisition. Participants will be presented with a series of learning tasks where they are required to categorize stimuli based on given rules or theories and the observable features of the stimuli. The experiment will manipulate the alignment or conflict between theoretical information and presented data to observe how participants integrate these sources of information when forming concepts. The replication will utilize a similar experimental design, employing PsychoPy and Pavlovia for data collection. This approach ensures methodological rigor while allowing for efficient, web-based participant recruitment and testing. By successfully replicating this study, the project will enhance the understanding of how humans learn and apply concepts, particularly in situations where theoretical expectations and empirical data interact.

title_r: Receptivity to Sexual Invitations
abstract_r: In a seminal study, Clark and Hatfield (1989) found that men were more willing than women to accept casual sexual invitations, whereas no significant gender differences were observed in responses to propositions for non-committal social activities. The present research comprises two preregistered naturalistic replication studies (total N = 240). Study 1 serves as a direct replication, while Study 2 additionally tests whether differences in sociosexuality account for why men are more willing than women to accept casual sexual offers. In both studies, men more readily than women accepted a sexual invitation from a stranger of the opposite gender. In contrast to the original study, the gender difference was independent of the type of proposition. Individual differences in sociosexuality did not account for the observed gender differences. In summary, gender differences in the willingness to accept casual sexual invitations persist to this day, over 40 years after the initial Clark and Hatfield study.

title_r: Do environmental messages emphasising binding morals promote conservatives’ pro-environmentalism? A pre-registered replication
abstract_r: Past studies indicated that environmental messages incorporating binding morals (i.e., loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, purity/degradation morals) were effective in reducing the negative association between political conservatism and pro-environmentalism. We conceptually replicated and extended this finding through open science practices. In a pilot study, we constructed three environmental messages incorporating each binding moral based on previous relevant studies, and confirmed their validity (96 U.S. adults, 50% woman). We then investigated the independent effects of these binding moral messages on pro-environmentalism across the political spectrum (705 U.S. adults, 56.6% woman). Contrasting with our expectations and previous findings, we found no evidence that these environmental messages emphasising distinct binding morals were more effective than a control environmental message in attenuating the political polarisations on conservation intentions and willingness to receive more information about environmental protection. Simply adding binding morals content in environmental messaging may not be useful in promoting conservatives’ pro-environmental engagement. We further discussed future research as well as limitations of this research.

title_r: The near-miss effect in online slot-machine gambling : a series of conceptual replications
abstract_r: The field of gambling studies is beginning to recognize the need to conduct targeted replications of influential effects throughout the field. Given the limited resources afforded to researchers, we must be systematic in our approach to selecting which effects are most in need of replication. Following a systematic approach to replication selection, a series of conceptual replications of the ‘near-miss effect’ in slot machine gambling was conducted, on online community samples. Near-miss outcomes on a slot machine are those that appear proximal to a win, though they are functionally identical to other losing outcomes (herein termed ‘full misses’). Near-misses have been shown to elicit a range of differential psychological effects compared to full-misses. Experiment 1a and 1b attempted to replicate a previous study by Clark et al. 2009 that 1) near-misses are experienced as more negative, 2) near-misses are rated as more motivating to continue playing a slot machine. Experiment 2 tested the effects on speed of gambling (a replication of Dixon et al. 2013) that near-miss outcomes speed up participant speed of play compared to full miss outcomes. Experiment 3 tested whether near-miss outcomes influence subsequent bet size. I replicated the motivation hypothesis of Clark et el., (2009), but found a significant effect in the opposite direction for the valence hypothesis. Across both study 1a and 1b, near-miss outcomes were more positive relative to full-misses. Experiment 2 replicated the hypothesis that near-miss outcomes increase speed of play (Dixon et al., 2013). Experiment 3 observed near-miss outcomes led to a significant increase in bet size on the subsequent spin relative to full-miss outcomes. I consider how this pattern of results across 3 different dependent variables speak to the different theoretical accounts of how near-misses operate.

title_r: S1 File -
abstract_r: <div><p>Childfree individuals, who are also described as ‘childless by choice’ or ‘voluntarily childless’, have decided they do not want biological or adopted children. This is an important population to understand because its members have unique reproductive health and end-of-life needs, and they encounter challenges managing work-life balance and with stereotypes. Prior estimates of childfree adults’ prevalence in the United States, their age of decision, and interpersonal warmth judgements have varied widely over time and by study design. To clarify these characteristics of the contemporary childfree population, we conduct a pre-registered direct replication of a recent population-representative study. All estimates concerning childfree adults replicate, boosting confidence in earlier conclusions that childfree people are numerous and decide early in life, and that parents exhibit strong in-group favoritism while childfree adults do not.</p></div>

summary: Implicit Candidate Traits in the 2016 Presidential Election: Evidence From a Nationally Representative Sample

Joseph A. Vitriol
Aleks Ksiazkiewicz
Christina E. Farhart 

Abstract
A major challenge to understanding how citizens assess political candidates, and how these assessments translate into political judgment and behavior, is the extent to which socially and politically relevant psychological processes and attitudinal evaluations are accessible at the conscious versus unconscious level. The current research seeks additional evidence for our dual-process model of candidate trait perceptions (Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart R&R) using a nationally representative sample in the context of the 2016 U.S. Presidential elections. We expect that implicit evaluations of the warmth and competence of major party candidates, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, would predict candidate evaluations, economic attitudes, vote intentions, and actual vote behaviors in the 2016 election. Consistent with prior research, we expect these implicit constructs (measured in September 2016) to demonstrate predictive validity for vote choice in the 2016 Presidential Election, above and beyond explicit analogs, demographics variables, partisan identification and ideological self-placement. We also expect these effects to be moderated by strength of partisan identification and strength of candidate preferences, which was measured in July of 2016.  Further, we explore additional potential moderators (e.g., gender bias; attitude certainty; cognitive style) and mediators for the correspondence between implicit-explicit attitudes (e.g., information search/exposure) to better understand the condition under which implicit constructs show incremental effects above and beyond explicit judgments. 

Keywords:  IAT, gender, vote choice, implicit warmth and competence, election
 

Implicit Candidate Traits in the 2016 Presidential Election: Evidence From a Nationally Representative Sample
	Research in political science investigating voter decision-making has traditionally assumed that voters have introspective access to their attitudes, preferences, and beliefs when making an electoral decision. However, much research in social psychology indicates that many types of cognitive processes, associations, and structures that give rise to attitudinal preferences are inaccessible to conscious awareness, either because such mental content is operating at the unconscious level or because it cannot be retrieved through deliberate introspection (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977; Winkielman & Schooler, 2011). A major challenge to understanding how citizens assess political candidates, and how these assessments translate into political judgment and behavior, is the extent to which socially and politically relevant psychological processes and attitudinal evaluations are accessible at the conscious versus unconscious level. 
	Political psychologists have begun to supplement theories of conscious, explicit processes with theories regarding unconscious, implicit processes in voter decision-making (e.g., Lodge & Taber, 2013; for a review of implicit research as it applies to political topics, see Ksiazkiewicz & Hedrick 2013). For example, in the 2012 Presidential Election, we examined the unique effects of implicit and explicit trait (i.e., Warmth and Competence) judgments on vote choice and evaluations of the presidential candidates, Barack Obama and Mitt Romney, in the 2012 US election. This line of inquiry suggests that 1) implicit candidate trait associations demonstrate predictive validity above and beyond its explicit counterpart, and 2) implicit trait associations are more consequential for undecided voters. This work is currently under review (Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart, revise and resubmit). However, this previous study relied upon a convenience sample, so its generalizability to representative samples is untested. 
	The current study seeks to extend and replicate our dual-process model of trait perceptions to a large sample weighted to be nationally representative and recruited in the context of the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election. First, we examine the incremental effect of implicit evaluations of the warmth and competence of major party candidates, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton, expecting these constructs to predict candidate evaluations, economic attitudes, vote intentions, and actual vote behaviors in the 2016 election above and beyond each other, explicit analogs, demographics variables, partisan identification and ideological self-placement. Second, consistent with previous research, we also expect these effects to be moderated by strength of partisan identification and strength of candidate preferences, which was measured in July of 2016.  Third, we explore potential moderators (e.g., gender bias; attitude certainty; cognitive style) and mediators for the correspondence between implicit-explicit attitudes (e.g., information search/exposure) to better understand the condition under which these implicit constructs show incremental effects above and beyond explicit judgments. 
	To our knowledge, few panel studies that include implicit measures has been undertaken to examine the effects of these constructs on changes in political judgment and behavior over the course of a political campaign (e.g., Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, & Farhart, revise and resubmit), and even fewer studies have included implicit measures in nationally representative samples. The broad aim of the current proposal is to advance the burgeoning literature on implicit processes in political contexts by investigating the consequences of implicit candidate-trait associations (i.e., using 2 versions of the Brief-IAT) on change in political attitudes and actual vote behavior in the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election using a large, national representative sample. 

Implicit Processes in Political Contexts
The study of implicit political attitudes and its electoral consequence can contribute to our understanding of the psychological processes that underlie voter decision-making in a number of ways. First, implicit associations are likely to account for unexplained variance in traditional models of voter decision-making. Implicit processes have incremental predictive validity across a wide range of domains traditionally examined exclusively at the explicit level (e.g., Greenwald Poehlman, Uhlmann, and Banaji 2009). In political contexts, implicit processes may be particularly useful for explaining the behavior of individuals whose behaviors are not well described by traditional political science theory (e.g., independents and undecided voters; Arcuri et al. 2008; Galdi, Arcuri, and Gawronski 2008; Galdi, Gawronski, Arcuri, and Friese 2012; Hawkins and Nosek 2012; but see Friese et al. 2012). 
Second, it is unlikely that this unexplained variance could be accounted for by traditional measurement techniques that focus exclusively on explicit attitudes. Implicit associations cannot be captured by traditional survey techniques because individuals are usually unaware of the impact of their implicit associations on their judgments and behaviors (Gawronski, Hofmann, and Wilbur 2006). Across a variety of domains, implicit processes have been shown to be related, but not reducible, to explicit processes (Hofmann et al., 2005; Nosek and Smyth 2007). Indeed, as demonstrated by meta-analysis (Greenwald et al. 2009), implicit and explicit measures of attitudes both show incremental predictive validity across behavioral domains, suggesting that each measure distinct psychological processes or cognitive structures that account for distinct portions of the variance in attitudinal and behavioral outcomes. 
Third, and most importantly for the current work, because implicit measures are largely unaffected by social desirability bias, they can be particularly useful in situations and on topics where traditional survey techniques may not capture participants’ “true” beliefs (Banse, Seise, & Zerbes, 2001; Boysen, Vogel, & Madon, 2006). For example, in the context of an election where at least one of the major party candidates is a woman, like the 2016 US presidential election, some voters may conceal their true assessments of candidates in order to appear unprejudiced (Redlawsk, Tolbert, and Franko 2010).  Similarly, some respondents may feel that it is socially undesirable to express support for Trump. 
Thus, implicit and explicit attitudes are not interchangeable, redundant constructs, but instead represent psychologically independent, and at times divergent (see Nosek 2005), attitudinal orientations that may have different evaluative and behavioral implications (e.g., Fazio 1990), even when no clear motivation for impression-management is present (e.g., Teubel, Asendorpf, Banse, and Schnabel 2011). Instead, automatic, unconscious associations may be incongruent with explicit attitudes and judgments. Accordingly, the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes may have important electoral consequences.

On the Correspondence Between Implicit and Explicit Attitudes
	Of central importance to the current investigation is the relation between implicit and explicit attitudes, as it speaks directly to the conditions under which and the individuals for whom unconscious associations matter. Meta-analytic investigations of implicit-explicit correspondence across a broad range of attitudinal domains generally indicate an average correlation that is positive and moderate (e.g., Nosek, 2005), but varies across content areas and individuals (Blair, 2001). Psychological factors that could potentially mediate the correspondence between implicit and explicit political attitudes remain largely unexamined.
	Implicit measures can be understood as capturing attitudinal preferences prior to the initiation of conscious, deliberative thought that could potentially change or “edit” individuals’ evaluation or response (Nosek, 2005). This suggests that attitudinally relevant cognitions and elaborations should increase the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes by increasing the likelihood that individuals obtain a more accurate conscious representation of their underlying implicit preferences, which should reduce its incremental predictive validity. Voters less interested in politics or who have weaker partisan identifications and candidate preferences are generally less likely to engage in the kind of cognitive elaboration that renders implicit and explicit attitudes highly congruent. For these individuals, we expect implicit candidate trait associations to demonstrate incremental predictive validity.
	Cognitive elaboration is expected to increase the correspondence between implicit and explicit attitudes because it increases the accessibility of underlying, unconscious preferences. Cognitive accessibility is indeed a critical psychological mechanism through which implicit associations may be incorporated into explicit judgments. Accordingly, we examine the possibility that individual differences associated with cognitive elaboration, including need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, and strength of partisan identification moderate the relationship between implicit and explicit trait associations for each candidate. Similarly, consistent with prior research on gender bias in warmth assessments (Winter, 2010), we expect that ambivalent sexism, separate spheres ideology, or negative explicit attitudes towards women (i.e., feeling thermometers) will moderate the relationship between implicit trait associations and actual vote behavior, such that implicit warmth assessments will matter more and implicit competence assessments will matter less for individuals characterized by gender bias.
	Finally, we also explore several behaviors that may reinforce implicit trait associations and therefore potentially mediate the relationship between these constructs and explicit attitudes and behavior. Specifically, we expect that implicit constructs will direct political engagement and participation, confirmatory information-search, biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks. These behaviors will, in turn, increase the likelihood that individuals’ explicit attitudes, behavioral intentions, and actual behaviors will be more consistent with the evaluative implications of the implicit constructs.
The Present Study
The major questions we address in this project is 1) if implicit trait associations shape explicit political judgment, preferences, and behavior (i.e., incremental predictive validity) for a nationally representative sample, 2) for whom (i.e., less politically knowledgeable, engaged, and interested members of the electorate; individuals engaged in low levels of cognitive elaboration; voters characterized by gender bias or not), and 3) what behaviors may mediate implicit-explicit congruence. We advance the following confirmatory hypotheses, based on the findings reported in Ksiazkiewicz, Vitriol, and Farhart (R&R). Below, we also advance several exploratory hypotheses, which are an extrapolation of prior research in psychology on implicit processes to the political domain:
1.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1: Implicit trait associations about candidate’s warmth and competence will independently predict explicit candidate evaluations and preferences, economic evaluations, behavioral intentions, and actual voting at the time of the election.
a.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1a: These effects of implicit constructs will emerge above/beyond demographics, explicit trait associations, partisan identification, and ideological self-placement.
b.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 1b: In addition to demographics, explicit candidate traits, partisan identification, and ideology, each implicit construct will demonstrate incremental validity independent of each other.
2.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2: Implicit trait associations about candidate’s warmth and competence will more strongly predict explicit candidate evaluations and preferences, economic evaluations, behavioral intentions, and actual voting at the time of the election among individuals with weak partisan identifications or candidate preferences.	
a.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2a: This interaction between implicit constructs and strength of attitudes and identification will emerge above/beyond demographics, explicit trait associations, and ideological self-placement.
b.	Confirmatory Hypothesis 2b: In addition to demographics, explicit candidate traits, partisan identification, and ideology, this interaction between each implicit constructs and strength of attitudes and identification will obtain significance when both implicit constructs are included in the model.
3.	Exploratory Hypothesis 1: Individual differences associated with cognitive elaboration, including need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, and strength of partisan identification, will moderate the relationship between implicit and explicit trait associations for each candidate, such that at high levels of cognitive elaboration implicit and explicit constructs will be more strongly related.
4.	Exploratory Hypothesis 2: Political engagement and participation, confirmatory information-search, biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks will mediate the relationship between implicit constructs and the likelihood that individuals’ explicit attitudes, behavioral intentions, and actual behaviors are more consistent with the evaluative implications of the implicit constructs.


Method
Data were collected as part of a large, multi-investigator panel study of the 2016 U.S. presidential election, utilizing a 4-wave panel design. At Wave 2, participants completed a warmth and competence IAT, in random order. The other measures used in this analysis were also administered to the same participants. Participants were recruited using Survey Sampling International.

Measures
All participants will complete a competence-IAT and warmth IAT, explicit measures of candidate trait evaluations, partisan identification and strength of partisan identification, need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge and interest, economic evaluations, candidate evaluations, vote preferences and choice,
political engagement and participation, media consumption and exposure, social network, ideological self-placement, and demographics. Below, we describe the implicit and explicit measures of candidate trait judgments and any additional transformations we intend to conduct on the variables. The appendix includes the language used to measure these other variables.

Measures
Implicit trait associations. The most commonly used method to measure implicit attitudes is a computer-administered categorization task, called the implicit association test (IAT, Greenwald, McGhee, and Schwartz 1998). Individuals are repeatedly presented with pairs of concepts and faster response latencies indicate stronger implicit associations between the concepts. Participants completed separate IATs at each wave for judgments of competence and warmth with a word-completion distractor task between the IATs. The order of the IATs was randomized for each respondent at the first wave and kept constant at subsequent waves. Each IAT paired adjectives categorized as warm or cold or as competent or incompetent with pictures of Obama and Romney.  These category labels were selected to reflect the underlying constructs of interest, as the choice of category labels on IATs has been found to affect measurement of implicit associations (Mitchell et al. 2003). Higher scores on each of these indicators represent stronger associations of the positive trait with Obama, relative to Romney. IAT scores were computed using the most recent algorithm from Greenwald, Nosek, and Banaji (2003).

Explicit trait judgments.
Explicit candidate-trait of warmth/competence were measuring using a single item. In some analyses, explicit candidate traits will be combined into a single variable if they are highly correlated, but not otherwise.

Data Analysis Plan
Survey weights 
We will follow the instructions provided by the survey research firm SSI to appropriately weight the data in all analyses.

Data Transformation 
IAT response times will be recoded into D-scores using the standard techniques (i.e., Greenwald, Nosek, & Banaji, 2003). D-scores will be recoded to run from -1 to 1, where 0 indicates no association, -1 indicates the theoretically maximal Hillary association (i.e., a D-score of -2) and 1 indicates the theoretically maximal Trump association (i.e., a D-score of 2). Vote choice will be analyzed in a number of ways. First, it will be dichotomized between Trump and Clinton (excluding others). Second, it will be treated as a multinomial logistic regression with categories including Trump, Clinton, third party, and not voting. Scale variables will be calculated as additive indexes. Candidate evaluations (e.g., feeling thermometers) will be differenced to provide a single scale (degree of preference for Trump/Hillary). All continuous and ordinal variables besides the IAT will be coded 0 to 1. Higher values will either indicate greater presence of the trait or greater Trump support/conservatism/Republicanism, as appropriate.


Hypothesis Testing
All models will include age, gender, race, and ideological self-placement as covariates. For analyses not utilizing partisan strength as a mediator/moderator, party ID will also be included as a covariate. For each set of analyses, we present four models, all of which include the aforementioned covariates. First, we regress dependent variables on implicit competence. Second, we regress dependent variables on implicit warmth. Third, we include both implicit warmth and competence in the model. Finally, we regress the dependent variables on the average of implicit warmth and competence (pooled implicit trait association). We present each of these models with and without covariates included. Below, we describe in greater detail how we intend to test each hypothesis.

Confirmatory hypothesis 1, 1a, 1b: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. For dependent variables that are measured repeatedly across waves, we will also explore the extent to which implicit constructs predict change by including lagged indicators of these dependent variables.

Confirmatory Hypothesis 2, 2a, 2b: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. In separate models, each implicit construct will be interacted with strength of partisanship or candidate preference. Simple slope analyses will be conducted at 1 SD Above/Below the mean of the moderator.

Exploratory Hypothesis 1: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories.  In separate models, each implicit regressors will be interacted with need to evaluate, need for cognition, need for closure, defensive confidence, political knowledge, and political interest. Simple slope analyses will be conducted at 1 SD Above/Below the mean of the moderator.

Exploratory Hypothesis 2: Weighted OLS regression will be used for differenced candidate evaluations, economic evaluations, and behavioral intentions. Voting will be analyzed using a probit model or multinomial probit model, depending on whether there are two categories or more than two categories. In separate models, the mediating role of 1) political engagement and participation, 2) confirmatory information-search, 3) biased consumption of attitudinally-congruent media, and 4) selection into politically homogenous (vs. heterogeneous) social networks will be tested separately for each implicit construct. Finally, mediation analyses were conducted by following the steps for bootstrapping recommended by Preacher & Hayes (2004; also see Zhao, Lynch, & Chen, 2010).

title_r: Improving the Replicability of Psychological Science Through Pedagogy
abstract_r: Replications are important to science, but who will do them? One proposal is that students can conduct replications as part of their training. As a proof-of-concept for this idea, here we report a series of 11 pre-registered replications of findings from the 2015 volume of Psychological Science, all conducted as part of a graduate-level course. Congruent with previous studies, replications typically yielded smaller effects than originals: The modal outcome was partial support for the original claim. This work documents the challenges facing motivated students in reproducing previously published results on a first attempt. We describe the workflow and pedagogical methods that were used in the class and discuss implications both for the adoption of this pedagogical model and for replication research more broadly.

title_r: Gender-fair language in German: An eye-tracking study on the readability of role nouns with special characters
abstract_r: The common traffic sign “Radfahrer bitte absteigen” (Cyclists [masc.] please dismount) illustrates the generic use of the masculine form in German. While the feminine form "Radfahrerinnen" refers to female cyclists only, the masculine "Radfahrer" may be used to refer specifically to male referents, or generically to persons of all genders, if gender is unknown or irrelevant to the context (cf. Gygax et al., 2019). However, multiple experimental studies have shown that the generically intended use of masculine forms leads to a substantial male bias (cf. Gygax et al., 2021). To counteract this bias, several gender-fair alternatives have been proposed. One binary alternative already introduced in the 1980s is the capital-I form (Binnen-I, e.g., RadfahrerInnen – feMale cyclists), aiming to increase the visibility of women. More recently, criticism of such binary forms has led to the development of more inclusive, non-binary forms (cf. Diewald & Steinhauer, 2017). The form that has recently gained significant traction (cf. Krome, 2020; Meuleneers, 2024) is the gender star form (Genderstern; Radfahrer*innen), where the asterisk aims to explicitly include individuals identifying beyond the female-male dichotomy. Initial studies suggest that the gender star reduces the male bias (e.g., Körner et al., 2022) and prompts more inclusive mental representations than the masculine form (Zacharski & Ferstl, 2023). Despite this, the German Council for Orthography (Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung, 2021) opposes both these gender-fair forms, arguing their not being in line with German orthography negatively affects the readability and comprehensibility of role nouns and texts. Indeed, for binary gender-fair forms that are not in line with the German orthography (such as the capital-I; hereafter: non-orthographic forms), research suggests that texts using gender-fair alternatives lead to significantly worse subjective ratings of readability (Pöschko and Prieler, 2018) and significantly longer full-text reading times (Blake and Klimmt, 2010) compared to the masculine form. For the non-binary gender star, however, Friedrich et al. (2021) found that subjective ratings of comprehensibility of students were worse only when the text contained predominantly singular forms, which require adaptations of articles and adjectives (e.g. der*die Spieler*in – the[masc.]*the[fem.] player[star]). In a similar study with a more diverse group of participants, Pabst & Kollmayer (2023) did not find any differences between subjective comprehensibility ratings for texts in masculine or star form when predominantly plural forms were used. While these studies provide valuable initial insights, they rely largely on subjective measures, which are prone to metacognitive influences such as the social desirability bias. Thus, experimental studies using more implicit measures are needed. Using a lexical decision task, a common implicit method to investigate lexical access, Zacharski et al. (2025) found that the gender star does not negatively influence the recognition of role nouns in students who were rather familiar with the gender star. In contrast, a group of older non-students showed initial difficulties in lexical access. However, these were overcome quickly over the course of the experiment. Based on the age-related effects, the authors concluded that readability of the non-orthographic star form might be a matter of familiarity and practice. Again, this study provides valuable insights; however, it remains on the word level. What is more, as the authors state, in order to further investigate the familiarity effect, it would be worthwhile to compare the readability of both the recently introduced gender star and the capital-I form, which has been in use for decades, as this might allow differentiating more thoroughly between the influences of orthography and familiarity. The implicit method of choice for investigating comprehension on the text level is eye-tracking, which offers detailed, real-time data on cognitive processing during reading, by recording eye-movements (cf. Rayner & Sereno, 1994; Schotter & Dillon, 2025). It is widely used in psycholinguistics and provides an objective measure of processing effort for pre-determined areas of interest (AoIs) within a text. We thus conducted a first experiment (hereafter: Experiment 1) with a sample of student participants (Zacharski et al., 2024). Herein, participants read 32 newspaper articles, of which 24 articles served as experimental items. Experimental texts included four tokens of the same role noun in either masculine, capital-I, or star form. The participants’ eye movements were recorded while reading. Moreover, they had to respond to a content question after each text. After all texts, they solved a memory task in which they had to recall the specific role nouns. Surprisingly, preliminary results revealed that the gender star did not impair the readability of texts – in contrast, it seemingly facilitated processing, compared to both the masculine and the capital-I form. Zacharski et al. (2024) suggested two possible explanations: On the one hand, the finding might be, again, due to the students’ familiarity with the form. On the other hand, it could be caused be the salience of the star form facilitating an immediate generic interpretation. Based on these preliminary results and following the suggestions by Zacharski et al. (2025), we conducted a second eye-tracking experiment (hereafter: Experiment 2), pre-registered here as a direct replication of the study presented by Zacharski et al. (2024). The study will involve a more diverse sample of non-student participants aged 40 to 70, aiming to disentangle potential effects of familiarity and orthography. This population is particularly interesting as it is likely that participants are familiar with the binary capital-I form, which was widely used from the 1980’s until recently, but less exposed to the now more prevalent non-binary gender star form. Accordingly, if the findings found in previous experiments are due to the readers’ familiarity with the gender star, participants may show different reading behaviour for the two forms. In addition, as in Experiment 1, we will conduct an exploratory analysis of participants’ attitudes not only toward gender-fair language in general, but also toward both non-binary and binary gender-fair forms (ABNBL; Zacharski, 2024). We are particularly interested in whether the reduced reading times observed for the gender star in Experiment 1 will be replicated in Experiment 2, whether the effect will instead be found only for the capital-I form, or whether both non-orthographic forms will lead to increased reading times. We also expect less positive attitudes toward gender-fair language in the older sample, possibly due to lower exposure in non-academic contexts (cf. Zacharski, 2024). The present dual-experiment study is the first to use eye-tracking to examine the readability of two non-orthographic gender forms, the binary capital-I form and the nonbinary gender star, at the text level, with both a young student sample (Experiment 1), and an older, non-student sample (Experiment 2).

title_r: Psychophysiological correlates of treatment effects – in search of potential biomarkers for the course of major depressive disorder
abstract_r: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is still one of the most common and highly debili-tating mental disorders. Although there are several treatment possibilities, the relapse rate is still high and some patients even suffer from treatment-resistant depression. First research re-sults suggest that the measurement of psychophysiological correlates (“biomarkers”) of MDD might be promising as a means to identify high-risk subgroups for poor outcomes in respect of MDD treatment. However, findings about the association between these correlates and MDD are still inconsistent, especially in naturalistic settings. To address this research gap, this dissertation focusses on assessing the explanatory value of psychophysiological correlates of depression to predict the course of MDD after inpa-tient treatment. This research employs two psychophysiological correlates of MDD that are typically used: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Cortisol Awakening Response (CAR). The overarching methodological goal that guided the studies within this dissertation is to use mul-tiple measurement designs to increase the robustness of psychophysiological data in naturalistic settings. Vagally-mediated HRV is seen as a psychophysiological marker for mental health and MDD. However, up to now, little has been known about the association between HRV and the severity of depression and whether this association mirrors treatment effects following in-patient psychotherapy. Therefore a multiple measurement study was conducted to assess the association between the severity of MDD symptoms and HRV before and after therapy. The sample consisted of 50 patients suffering from moderate to severe MDD. HRV was assessed three times at the beginning of, and three times at discharge from, inpatient psychotherapy. Depressive symptoms were assessed by self-reports (Beck Depression Inventory, BDI-II) and a third-party questionnaire (Hamilton rating scale for depression, HRSD) at the beginning of psychotherapy and at discharge. Results confirm an expected negative correlation between HRV and depressive symptoms at the beginning of the inpatient treatment. At discharge, results show a de-coupling between HRV and symptom severity: Depressive symptoms improve sig-nificantly (d=0.84) without corresponding changes in HRV as a psychophysiological indicator. CAR reflects a dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis which is associated with MDD. Initial research results suggest that CAR resembles the accumulated effects of MDD and therefore might be a predictor for the course of depression after discharge. Therefore CAR was measured at intake to inpatient psychotherapy. The BDI was assessed at IX four time-points (intake, discharge, 6 weeks after discharge and 6 months after discharge). The sample included 123 inpatients diagnosed with MDD. The results show that a blunted CAR at intake predicts mood deterioration six weeks and six months following discharge. Due to a lack of comparative data, and to verify these initial results regarding the association of CAR and MDD, a replication study was conducted. The replication study used an improved methodology with stricter assessment protocols and monitoring. The sample in-cluded 122 inpatients diagnosed with moderate to severe MDD. CAR and self-ratings were assessed at the same measurement points as in the original study. Results could be replicated in terms of nearly identical effect sizes but do not reach statistical significance (p=.054). The rep-lication of effect sizes with a concurrent lack of statistical significance may well inform re-search on psycho-endocrinological predictors for treatment success, but raises the question of practical relevance for CAR as a predictor for the further course of MDD. Results are discussed for each study individually and on an aggregate level with respect to the overarching research question. Taken together, they show that the associations between biological and psychological aspects are very complex and are influenced by many factors. Robust measurement designs are required to improve scientific understanding. However, when measured strictly, additional information regarding the association between biomarkers and the course of depression can be gathered. However, the explanatory power of a single biomarker seems to be too small to have clinical impact. Therefore biomarkers can be viewed only as an additional source of information to predict treatment effects.

title_r: Merging Structural and Process-Related Approaches to the Study of Agreeableness: A Preregistered Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Agreeableness is one of the major domains included within prominent hierarchical models of personality like the Five-factor Model (FFM). (Low) agreeableness has shown to be the strongest correlate of a variety of antisocial behaviors relative to the other FFM domains. Though there is substantial evidence that (low) agreeableness is arguably the most important personality correlate of various antisocial behaviors, this evidence is descriptive and provides little information on the direction or processes underlying the relation. Process-related research has started to provide more insight into how agreeableness-related traits give rise to various antisocial and prosocial behaviors. The proposed study looks to first replicate previous research on some of the potential cognitive/emotional processes related to agreeableness, and then to conduct exploratory analyses to identify which, if any, of the empirically identified facets of agreeableness bear specific relations to the processes under study. Thus, the proposed project seeks to merge developments across important domains of personality research, structural research and process-based research, while also making use of open-science practices.

title_r: Image1_Genetic association and transferability for urinary albumin-creatinine ratio as a marker of kidney disease in four Sub-Saharan African populations and non-continental individuals of African ancestry.PDF
abstract_r: Background<p>Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have predominantly focused on populations of European and Asian ancestry, limiting our understanding of genetic factors influencing kidney disease in Sub-Saharan African (SSA) populations. This study presents the largest GWAS for urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) in SSA individuals, including 8,970 participants living in different African regions and an additional 9,705 non-resident individuals of African ancestry from the UK Biobank and African American cohorts.</p>Methods<p>Urine biomarkers and genotype data were obtained from two SSA cohorts (AWI-Gen and ARK), and two non-resident African-ancestry studies (UK Biobank and CKD-Gen Consortium). Association testing and meta-analyses were conducted, with subsequent fine-mapping, conditional analyses, and replication studies. Polygenic scores (PGS) were assessed for transferability across populations.</p>Results<p>Two genome-wide significant (P < 5 × 10<sup>−8</sup>) UACR-associated loci were identified, one in the BMP6 region on chromosome 6, in the meta-analysis of resident African individuals, and another in the HBB region on chromosome 11 in the meta-analysis of non-resident SSA individuals, as well as the combined meta-analysis of all studies. Replication of previous significant results confirmed associations in known UACR-associated regions, including THB53, GATM, and ARL15. PGS estimated using previous studies from European ancestry, African ancestry, and multi-ancestry cohorts exhibited limited transferability of PGS across populations, with less than 1% of observed variance explained.</p>Conclusion<p>This study contributes novel insights into the genetic architecture of kidney disease in SSA populations, emphasizing the need for conducting genetic research in diverse cohorts. The identified loci provide a foundation for future investigations into the genetic susceptibility to chronic kidney disease in underrepresented African populations Additionally, there is a need to develop integrated scores using multi-omics data and risk factors specific to the African context to improve the accuracy of predicting disease outcomes.</p>

title_r: Image 2_Surrogate data analyses of the energy landscape analysis of resting-state brain activity.tif
abstract_r: The spatiotemporal dynamics of resting-state brain activity can be characterized by switching between multiple brain states, and numerous techniques have been developed to extract such dynamic features from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. However, many of these techniques are based on momentary temporal correlation and co-activation patterns and merely reflect linear features of the data, suggesting that the dynamic features, such as state-switching, extracted by these techniques may be misinterpreted. To examine whether such misinterpretations occur when using techniques that are not based on momentary temporal correlation or co-activation patterns, we addressed Energy Landscape Analysis (ELA) based on pairwise-maximum entropy model (PMEM), a statistical physics-inspired method that was designed to extract multiple brain states and dynamics of resting-state fMRI data. We found that the shape of the energy landscape and the first-order transition probability derived from ELA were similar between real data and surrogate data suggesting that these features were largely accounted for by stationary and linear properties of the real data without requiring state-switching among locally stable states. To confirm that surrogate data were distinct from the real data, we replicated a previous finding that some topological properties of resting-state fMRI data differed between the real and surrogate data. Overall, we found that linear models largely reproduced the first order ELA-derived features (i.e., energy landscape and transition probability) with some notable differences.

title_r: UNDERSTANDING THE STRUCTURE AND CORRELATES OF NON-RIGID SPATIAL SKILLS
abstract_r: We developed and tested a novel measure of non-rigid, ductile spatial skill using knot reasoning. In Study 1, 279 US adults (M = 30.90 SD = 5.47 years; 76% White, 48% women) recruited through Prolific completed a 73-item knot reasoning task. Using Item Response Theory, we tested the reliability of the measure and removed items with low discrimination to yield a final 54-item measure with good reliability (α = .88). In Study 2, 147 US adults (M = 20.65 SD = 2.80 years; 48% White, 56% women) recruited from a public university in the mid-Atlantic completed a battery of existing spatial skills measures, the new knot reasoning measure, a control verbal measure, and a survey of current and childhood spatial activities. We validated the knot reasoning measure: performance on this measure is significantly, positively correlated with existing measures of spatial skill (mental rotation, paper folding, bending). However, we did not find support for a continuum of spatial skills from non-rigid to rigid using a simultaneous regression and a confirmatory factor analytic approach. Finally, we replicated prior work showing a male advantage in mental rotation performance but no gender differences in other spatial skills, though this relationship differed when using a modeling approach that incorporated spatial activities experience. Using a structural equation modeling approach, we found that masculine-stereotyped spatial activities engagement mediated the relationship between gender and mental rotation and knot reasoning task performance, where men who reported fewer spatial activities had higher spatial skills. Current and childhood feminine-stereotyped spatial engagement mediated the relationship between gender and paper folding performance, with women who reported greater spatial activities had higher spatial skills. Finally, we found that spatial skills did not differ among math-intensive STEM, non-math-intensive STEM, and non-STEM majors.

title_r: Numerical modelling of the lobes of radio galaxies -- Paper V: Universal Pressure Profile cluster atmospheres
abstract_r: We present relativistic magnetohydrodynamic modelling of jets running into hydrostatic, spherically symmetric cluster atmospheres. For the first time in a numerical simulation, we present model cluster atmospheres based upon the Universal Pressure Profile (UPP), incorporating a temperature profile for a typical self-similar atmosphere described by only one parameter - $M_{500}$. We explore a comprehensive range of realistic atmospheres and jet powers and derive dynamic, energetic and polarimetric data which provide insight into what we should expect of future high-resolution studies of AGN outflows. From the simulated synchrotron emission maps which include Doppler beaming we find sidedness distributions that agree well with observations. We replicated a number of findings from our previous work, such as higher power jets inflating larger aspect-ratio lobes and the cluster environment impacting the distribution of energy between the lobe and shocked regions. Comparing UPP and $β$-profiles we find that the cluster model chosen results in a different morphology for the resultant lobes with the UPP more able to clear lobe material from the core; and that these different atmospheres influence the ratio between the various forms of energy in the fully developed lobes. This work also highlights the key role played by Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instabilities in the formation of realistic lobe aspect-ratios. Our simulations point to the need for additional lobe-widening mechanisms at high jet powers, for example jet precession. Given that the UPP is our most representative general cluster atmosphere, these numerical simulations represent the most realistic models yet for spherically symmetric atmospheres.

title_r: What UAE Software Students Think about Software Testing: A Replicated Study
abstract_r: Software testing is vital to improve software quality. However, software tester role is stigmatized, partly due to misperception and partly due to the treatment of the testing process within the software industry. The present study analyses this situation aiming to explore what might inhibit an individual from taking up a software testing career. In order to investigate this issue, we surveyed 132 senior students pursuing degrees in information systems, information and communication technology, computer science, computer engineering, software engineering, and other closely-related disciplines at three universities in the United Arab Emirates: two publicly funded and one top-notch private university. The students were asked to describe the PROs and CONs of taking up a career in software testing and to ponder the likelihood that they would take up the career themselves. The study identified 7 main PROs and 9 main CONSs for pursuing a testing career, and indicated that the role of software tester is perceived as a social role, which may require as many soft skills as technical prowess. The results also show that UAE software-related students have a stronger negative attitude towards software testing compared to their counterparts in other countries where similar investigations have been carried out in the past three years.

title_r: Exploring the adoption of symptom-assessment applications in Germany: An investigation of awareness, use, and usefulness
abstract_r: Background: Symptom-assessment applications (SAAs) allow laypeople to obtain advice on whether and where they should seek medical care, along with possible diagnoses. Although their average accuracy is currently far from perfect, SAAs might in fact have the potential to unburden healthcare systems. Previous studies from the United States and the United Kingdom indicate that users of these systems are mostly young, female, and well-educated. However, data on SAA awareness in Germany is scant. Thus, this thesis aims to assess the extent of awareness, use and perceived usefulness of SAAs in a German sample and to explore how different respondent characteristics are associated with them. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey, with 1,084 German respondents stratified to reflect the German population. They were asked several questions involving individual characteristics, as well as questions about their knowledge and use of SAAs and their perception of SAA usefulness. The collected data were analyzed exploratively. Results: Respondent awareness of SAAs was 16.3% and respondent rate of using SAAs 6.5%. Among those who were aware of SAAs, 40.1% had used them. Of those, 40.8% considered SAAs useful. Users were on average younger (M = 37.6, SD = 14.3) than nonusers (M = 47.3, SD = 15.8), more often female (62.0% among users vs. 50.9% among nonusers), and well educated (42.3% with a university or college degree vs. 27.6%). Similar characteristics were observed for those who were aware of SAAs. However, these characteristics did not differ between users and respondents who were aware of SAAs but did not use them. Knowing about the existence of SAAs was associated with the use of other eHealth applications (r = .23) and knowing about digitale Gesundheitsanwendungen (DiGA) (r = .13) and the elektronische Patientenakte (ePA) (r = .11). Using SAAs was associated with using other health apps (r = .25), DiGA (r = .19) and ePA (r = .22), but not with being aware of these applications (r = -.05 and r = -.08, respectively). Discussion: The data from our study suggests a slightly lower number of SAA users in Germany—yet at the same time twice as many respondents who were aware of the existence of SAAs—than a previous study did. We replicated results from previous studies (that found users to be younger, more often female, and well educated) and extended these findings by showing that these characteristics are associated with awareness of SAAs but not with SAA use itself. The data also indicates the existence of two separate concepts regarding eHealth technologies: Knowing about these technologies and using them. This difference should be considered in future studies when interpreting data on characteristics of SAA and eHealth users. Ultimately, to maximize SAA potential and its ability to support the public, approaches should be devised that would reach those who might benefit from the technologies but who are currently unaware of their existence.

title_r: Follow-up to https://osf.io/fv6yn
abstract_r: The current study is a follow-up to a previous study registered as “Information search in complex decisions from experience” (https://osf.io/fv6yn). As the follow-up largely follows the protocol of the original study, we refer to the original preregistration where possible. Summary of the original study: In decisions from experience, people can learn about the options’ payoff distributions via sampling (ecological search). However, because sampling does not give direct access to summary descriptions of the distributions’ properties, the mind needs to actively form such representations by further processing the samples (cognitive search). When given a decision goal that requires the comparison of a particular property of the distributions, do people adopt an ecological search pattern that organizes the samples in a way that reduces the number of required processing steps (i.e., cognitive search costs) and thus facilitates achieving the decision goal? We instructed participants to either choose the option with better short-term or long-term rewards and tested whether they systematically adopt their ecological search pattern in terms of switching more or less frequently between options. The results show that the choice performance (i.e., achieving the instructed decision goal) indeed depended on participants’ switching behavior: Participants with higher switch rates are better at identifying the short-term winner, but worse at identifying the long-term winner. Most of all, participants seemed to be sensitive to this relation and switched more frequently in the short-term than in the long-term winner condition, indicating adaptive search. Aim of the follow-up: The original study showed that people's sampling behavior (switch rate) is adaptive. However, the difference in switch rates between the short-term and long-term winner condition was small (Mean difference = .06 , 95%-PI = [.05;.08]). Moreover, we varied the complexity of choice problems in the original study, assuming that the cognitive search costs increase with higher complexity, making search adaptation more important. In line with this intuition, switch rates indeed had a considerably stronger effect on choice performance in more complex choice problems. However, the difference in switch rates between the short-term and long-term winner condition did not get larger. Thus, people's sampling behavior was only adaptive to a limited extent. In the follow-up, we aim to replicate the the core findings from the original study that decision goals affect switch rates -- i.e., participants asked to identify the option with higher short-term rewards should switch more frequently than the participants asked to identify the option with higher long-term rewards. Moreover, we want to investigate two potential causes that might have limited the adaptivity of the switching behavior. First, in the original study, there were higher costs attached to switching between options relative to staying on the same option (because staying required no mouse movevement but switching did). These motion costs of switching might explain the overall low switch rates as well as why participants in the short-term winner condition had only slightly higher switch rates than participants in the short-term winner condition. In the follow-up, we investigate this effect by eliminating the motion costs of switching (i.e., after each sample, the mouse is set back to neutral position between options). Second, in the original study, people did not receive direct feedback on whether they made the correct or wrong decision in a given choice problem. This might have prevented participants to learn the relation between the way they organize their information search (i.e., their switch rate) and their ability to achieve their decision goal. In the follow-up, we include a training phase for half of the participants, in which participants receive direct feedback on their choice performance after each choice.

title_r: Ratio format shapes health decisions: The practical significance of the “1-in-X” effect.
abstract_r: Prior research found that “1-in-X” ratios led to higher and less accurate subjective probability than “N-in-X*N” ratios or other formats even though they featured the same mathematical information. It is unclear, however, whether the effect transfers into health decisions and the practical significance of the effect is undetermined. Based on previous findings and risk communication theories, we hypothesised that the “1-in-X” effect would occur and transfer into relevant decisions. We also tested whether age, gender and education differences would moderate the “1-in-X” effect on decision-making. We conducted three well-powered experiments (n = 1912) using a sample from the general adult UK population to test our hypotheses, estimated the effect and excluded a possible methodological explanation for such a transfer. In hypothetical scenarios, participants decided whether to travel to Kenya given the chance of contracting malaria (Experiment 1) and whether to take recommended steroids given the side effects (Experiments 2 and 3). Across the experiments, we replicated a small-to-medium “1-in-X” effect on the perceived probability, Hedge’s g = -0.36, 95% CI [-0.47, -0.24], z = -6.18, p < .001 and found a small effect on subsequent decisions, OR = 1.32, 95% CI [1.10, 1.59], z = 2.99, p = .003. The perceived probability fully mediated the effect of the ratio format on decision. Age, gender and education did not moderate the “1-in-X” effect on decision. We argue that a high prevalence of “1-in-X” ratios in medical communication makes these small changes clinically relevant. Therefore, to communicate information accurately, “1-in-X” ratios should not be used or at least used cautiously in medical communication.

title_r: Confirmation bias: Snyder & Swann (1978) 40 years later
abstract_r: Building on the seminal work of Snyder and Swann (1978), the aim of the present study is to provide new evidence for the hypothesis-confirming bias. In Snyder and Swann’s article (Study 2, 1978), participants had to investigate if another participant was extraverted or introverted. For that purpose, participants were paired and each was assigned either the role of “interviewer” or the role of “target”. Half of the interviewer-participants were instructed to assess to what extent the target was extraverted and the other half were instructed to assess to what extent the target was introverted. After receiving the instructions, they had to select a limited number of questions to ask the target out of a large set of questions biased either in favor of extraversion or in favor of introversion (plus unrelated questions). After this question-selection phase, target-participants were tape recorded while answering the questions selected by the interviewer. Then, interviewer-participants and external judges had to rate the target-participants on personality traits related to extraversion-introversion. The authors showed that interviewer-participants appear to have formulated confirmatory hypothesis-testing strategies (i.e. they selected more extraverted questions when they were instructed to investigate whether the target was extraverted and similarly for introversion). In other words, data shows a confirmation bias in the search of information. Moreover, in the second stage of the experiment, they demonstrated that target participants tended to behave in a consistent way with the hypothesis of the interviewer-participants (behavioral confirmation effect). We already have conducted two preregistered studies (Study 1: https://osf.io/w3n9p/?view_only=c4c6ab40021f4713bbe13f7b70d6e968 – Study 2: https://osf.io/32gmr/?view_only=f08f06272add4cd6ba81faeeadc57cd5) to replicate and extend Snyder and Swann (1978) effects. Our aims were to replicate the confirmatory hypothesis-testing in the search of information and to extend this effect testing and to extend it to judgment (in an impression formation task). These 2 first studies ‘designs were highly inspired by studies from Snyder & Swann (1978) but with a few differences: a) all participants were assigned the interviewer role and the target was fictitious and b) participants received feedback (ambiguous on the dimensions of extraversion/introversion) regardless of their experimental condition. In this first study, we replicated the effect of hypothesis confirmation in seeking information (i.e., in the "choice of questions'' task). However, on the evaluation of the target (i.e., the impression formation task), the results were unexpected. We observed that participants who were to test the extraversion hypothesis judged the target as more introverted than participants in the introversion condition. In the second study, we added a condition. We propose that the effect on the first task (i.e., the choice of questions) is an effect of experimental demand and that participants had no expectations/hypothesis regarding the level of introversion/extraversion of the target. Without a clear hypothesis in mind, participants may have intended to remain as neutral as possible leading to a counter-regulation effect (Rothermund, 2011). In other words, participants exposed to positive information (i.e., extraverted condition) or negative ones (i.e., introverted condition) may have focused more on information of opposite valence to regulate their affective-motivational sate which impacted target evaluation. We therefore sought to get participants to have a hypothesis to test in mind by giving them more information (vs. not). For half of participants, in an attempt to reinforce the hypothesis testing instruction, we added statistical information (i.e., a paragraph stating that the majority of psychology students are introverted or extraverted depending on their experimental condition). The statistical information was in all the cases congruent with the given hypothesis (i.e., extraversion vs. introversion). When no information was given, we replicated the results of the first study. However, when we gave the statistical information, we observed the opposite pattern. Participants testing introversion did find the target to be more introverted than participants testing extraversion. A hypothesis about mechanism underlying confirmation effects is that confirmation bias is a specific case of goal pursuit. Participants did seek to confirm their initial hypothesis by activating the goal of evaluating the target through responses to questions. Thus, one possible explanation for our previous studies effects could rely on the delay between the instruction and the task. Bargh, Lee-Chai, Barndollar, Gollwitzer, & Trötschel (2001) showed that when the activation of a goal and its execution were separated by a delay (i.e., a task unrelated to the goal) the action associated with the goal was performed with more attention (i.e., in their study, better performance). In contrast, the activation of a goal on a task associated with this goal but which would not be behavioral per se (e.g., an impression formation task) would be less important after a delay or even disappear. In their Experiment 3, the authors activated the performance goal non-consciously by priming (vs. no goal - control condition). Participants then had to either directly perform the target task (no delay) or perform a task before the target task (delay). The target task was either a direct performance task (word puzzle task) or a performance-related impression formation task (i.e., is Donald performing well?). In the performance goal condition, and when the target task was delayed, participants performed better on the word-puzzle task and evaluated the target more negatively on the impression formation task. The authors propose that this is related to the type of priming (construal vs. behavioral priming). Motivational constructs lead to an increase in the strength of goal-directed action tendencies (Atkinson & Birch, 1970; i.e., behavioral priming). Perceptual (or non-motivational) constructs related to the activated goal, on the other hand, should decrease over time (e.g., Anderson, 1983; Higgins, Bargh, & Lombardi, 1985). In the case of our first study, we might have activated, through our instructions, a conscious goal of evaluating the target through his responses to questions (e.g., Chartrand, Cheng, Dalton, & Tesser, 2010). Thus, the text-based evaluation task would have fulfilled the role of an interfering task, since the evaluation is not based on the answers to the questions selected by the participant. Because the evaluation task is an impression formation task and not directly behavioral, it could explain the reversed pattern of results with respect to the activated goal. In the case of our second study, when we gave participants statistical information, we could have created a supra-ordinate goal (i.e., validated the statistical information) which could explain why the effects appeared consistent with the hypothesis confirmation effect (e.g., Moors, Boddez, & De Houwer, 2017). Here we propose to conduct a third experiment in which we would manipulate the delay. Participants will have the goal to evaluate a target, without using questions, contrary to our previous experiments. For half of them, we will set up an interfering task (unrelated to the goal). We expect a hypothesis confirmation bias when the task is performed directly (i.e., without a delay) whereas we expect to replicate the reverse pattern obtained in our two previous studies when participants perform the task after the interfering task (i.e., with a delay). An alternative explanation could be that we activated a behavioral motivation (i.e., the behavior of providing an evaluation) but did not allow participants to produce a behavior. In this case, we should observe an even larger hypothesis confirmation effect after a delay. However, this hypothesis seems less plausible in view of the literature on goal activation and impression formation, which is described in terms of attitude and evaluation rather than behavior (e.g., Bargh, Lombardi, & Higgins, 1985; 1988; Bargh, Bond, Lombardi, & Tota, 1986; Higgins, 1989; 1996; Srull & Wyer, 1979). The confirmation of our hypothesis could imply that confirmation bias is an instance of goal pursuit mechanisms (although other processes may be at work) and thus apply to tasks other than question selection or impression formation.
